#3170. After FAA Ground Stop, John Oliver Compares Trump Cabinet Official To “A Batman Villain Trying To Hold Gotham Hostage”

On Sunday’s Last Week Tonight, John Oliver channeled the anger felt by millions of Americans at last week’s nationwide FAA ground stop.

Oliver noted that official information was fairly scarce during most of the five hours when some 3,500 planes were grounded. He then suggested that, when they finally did appear on TV, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin weren’t quite up to the task of explaining the situation to Americans.

After calling Mullin a “moron,” Oliver had this for Duffy: “Rather than use that press conference to dispense information, which would have been ideal, he instead took it as an opportunity to air grievances and make demands.” Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Networks Scramble To Report On Reasons Behind "Extraordinary" Nationwide Ground Stop Of All U.S. Flights News John Oliver Unleashes Withering Critique Of Pete Hegseth On 'Last Week Tonight'

“What went down was old. It was old, legacy equipment that failed,” said the secretary. “And, listen, it’s going to continue to fail…The president for the last year has been asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system…The president’s asked for $30B. I want $50B. I can’t build things if i don’t have money…I want &50B. President Trump is a builder. He is going to build this network for the American people.”

“What are you doing going on TV to demand $50B?!” he asked. “You sound less like a secretary of transportation trying to calm people down and more like a Batman villain trying to hold Gotham hostage! ‘I need $50B unless the Batman can solve my riddles in time!'”

Oliver admitted that Duffy is right about one thing: U.S. flight systems are outdated. But the Last Week Tonight host pointed out that Republicans have had both houses of Congress (and the presidency) for the past two years, so if there’s a complaint about underfunding, it should land on their collective doorstep. He also pointed out that the Republican Congress and the administration collaborated to nearly triple ICE’s budget last year to $28B, an amount that surpasses the annual budgets of almost all other major federal law enforcement agencies combined.

“It is hard to take a panicked shakedown from Duffy, not just because his cost estimate jumped by $20B mid-sentence, but also because he’s part of a flagrantly-corrupt administration who spent a chunk of his time in office shooting a shitty reality show with his family to encourage Americans to take more road trips.” [Duffy, his wife and their nine kids shot The Great American Road Trip over seven months this year and last.]

“To that end,” said Oliver in reference to both the show and the recent flight stoppage, “guess what, Sean? Mission f*cking accomplished!”

As First World problems go, losing your evening to non-committal HBO Max scrolling isn't ideal. It's way too easy to just stick on your 14th "The Sopranos" rewatch on the HBO streaming service, rather than give a potential sci-fi classic you've never seen before a much-deserved (and overdue) viewing.

That's where my obsessive cinephile colleagues and I are here for. We all watch movies with great passion. For me, it's what gets me out of bed in the morning. Though I don't always personally agree with Rotten Tomatoes ratings — how is "The Matrix" only at 83%?! — the trio of HBO Max pictures I've picked out for you are all excellent, and all scored at least 90% or higher.

Anyway, the following three sci-fi flicks are all streaming now on HBO Max, and each one is stellar. So get them watched ASAP.

It's utterly appalling that I only saw “2001: A Space Odyssey” for the first time post-COVID. Stanley Kubrick’s seminal sci-fi opus is a mind-bending watch in the best possible way. It looks incredible, the final act is both spellbinding and slightly mystifying, and it easily boasts one of the most iconic scores of all time.

It’s a five-star masterpiece. Yet I shamefully knew of it first for cheeky references in 1994’s “Deep Space Homer” episode from our beloved Springfieldian family, then again during 2023’s “Barbie”, which features a lovely, genuinely funny callback to the iconic monolith scene. And I’d never seen the film at that point! Shameful!

Just know that this is the defining Kubrick masterpiece. HAL! Those apes getting comfy up against the monolith! The all-time iconic final scene with the space baby! I know I said it before, but “seminal” really is the only word to describe “2001: A Space Odyssey”. It’s arguably the most important and influential sci-fi movie ever made. RT is doing Kubrick's opus dirty at ‘just’ a 91% rating.

Rotten Tomatoes score: 91%Watch “2001: A Space Odyssey” on HBO Max now

I’m fond of “Dune: Part Two”, just as I was of its 2021 predecessor — two movies that pretty much erased David Lynch’s polarizing 1984 version from memory banks. And Lynch rarely dealt in duds. Though I don’t consider him at the level of legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins (an occasional Denis Villeneuve collaborator), Greig Fraser still shoots the mid-part of this epic sci-fi trilogy gorgeously.

Do I think “Dune: Part Two” is as good a picture as either Villeneuve’s 2016 “Arrival" (91% RT rating) or my beloved "Blade Runner 2049" (88% RT)? Hell no. But it’s a classy sci-fi sequel that has me all in on this December’s Dunesday.

I can’t lie, though. I do think "Part Two" misses the wonderful presence of Duncan Idaho (Jason Momoa). But hey, we still get those colossal sandworms. And new Big Bad Feyd-Rautha Harkonnen (played with a delicious serpent-like venom by Austin Butler) proves a great foil for Paul Atredides. As for our moody duke, Timothée Chalamet continues to nail down his leading man status in films with real smarts.

Rotten Tomatoes score: 92%Watch "Dune: Part Two" on HBO Max now

Can you quickly indulge me in a quick Rotten Tomatoes rant? The fact that “Dawn of the Planet of the Apes” is sitting on the same 91% rating as my favourite ever movie “Jurassic Park”... well, that’s frankly unhinged. The sequel to 2011’s successful franchise reboot “Rise of the Planet of the Apes”, “Dawn” is another well-meaning sci-fi with a heart, strong performances and excellent effects. It just ain’t Spielberg’s dino masterpiece. Rant over.

With our simian hero Caesar (another impeccable mo-cap performance from Andy Serkis) now very much in charge of his clan of developed apes, the film’s central conflict occurs when a team of humans tries to repair a hydroelectric dam in monkey territory. Although initial exchanges go badly, the kindly-natured super chimp eventually lets Malcolm (a very good Jason Clarke) fix the dam, and a cross-species friendship quickly ensues. However, thanks to the war-mongering antics of Gary Oldman’s Dreyfus and chimp backstabbing courtesy of Caesar’s chum Kobo — Toby Kebbell’s mo-cap turn is on par with Serkis’ — all-out war breaks out across a dystopian San Francisco. And the apes definitely have our number.

#3168. iOS 27.2 has two CarPlay improvements, here’s what’s new

iOS 27.2 arrived last month with new features for Messages, Apple TV, and more, plus two improvements for CarPlay. Here’s what’s new for CarPlay users.

Apple Podcasts in iOS 27.2 adds two new sections to the Home tab: ‘New Episodes’ and ‘Continue Playing.’

Essentially, Apple has rethought how the core ‘Up Next’ queue of its Podcasts app works.

Like you would expect, ‘New Episodes’ contains only the latest episodes from your favorite shows. But after you’ve started an episode, you’ll find it in the ‘Continue Playing’ row just below.

This overhaul to podcast management makes it easier to find the latest episodes of your shows and also pick up where you previously left off. I’m a big fan of the change.

Siri AI introduces a variety of upgrades in iOS 27.2, including two that carry over to CarPlay as well.

It can take some adjustment to remember that Siri AI is available in the car just like on iPhone. But CarPlay is an especially useful platform for Apple’s more powerful assistant.

It’s arguable whether this qualifies as an “improvement,” but it is a change worth mentioning. iOS 27.2 includes a new app icon for Apple Music, plus some minor design tweaks in the app.

These changes are related to the broader rebrand of Apple Music that was recently unveiled.

For more new features in CarPlay that debuted in iOS 27, see our coverage here.

#3165. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

Don’t try this at home: To better understand the risk AI slop poses to scientific publishing today, IEEE Spectrum contributor Benjamin Skuse put IEEE’s research integrity checks to the test by submitting two entirely AI-generated papers. “Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

Could community colleges help fill the coming talent shortage in the U.S. semiconductor industry? Alternatives to four-year university degrees are a promising option for the technicians who will be needed to run new fabs.

#3164. Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving

iOS 27 gave Apple Maps a handful of new features, and my favorite is one that keeps offering fresh updates every week: Local Lists.

Apple Maps has long offered a ‘Guides’ feature where you can browse curated collections of places worth checking out. Sometimes they’re created by Apple’s editorial team, other times by celebrities or in conjunction with current events.

But in iOS 27, there’s a new feature—Local Lists—that’s sort of an extension of Guides, but it gets updated weekly with the latest trending places.

Here’s how Apple describes it, via Apple Newsroom:

I’ve always enjoyed browsing Guides in Maps to help find new places. But Local Lists are a great expansion of the idea, especially since they’re updated all the time. I’m always up for trying a new trending restaurant, and now Maps makes it easy to stay on top of what’s new.

Even if you’ve been using iOS 27 for months, there’s a good chance you’ve never seen Local Lists. That’s because they’re pretty hidden.

To find the feature, tap into the search field in Maps and scroll down to see a new ‘Trending Restaurants’ section. On my iPhone 18 Pro, by default this section gets hidden behind the keyboard, so you have to first scroll and dismiss the keyboard to see it.

Trending Restaurants are ranked from 1-20. The search screen shows only a handful, but you can tap to view the full list. For example, if you open the ‘Trending Restaurants in New York’ list, you’ll see 20 places worth checking out.

How does a restaurant make the list? Per the in-app explanation, the list contains “Restaurants climbing in popularity this week, based on what people view, share, and interact with on Apple Maps.”

Yeah still not my go to navigation option. Until they can give users the amount of information / detail / items to mark and make its alerts functioning like Waze, it won't really be much of a competitor. This stuff if great to have but why Would I want to keep switching between apps to get different information.

Maybe in 3-5 years their engineering team will mimic Waze and treat it like they've just discovered something great😒🤣

Since these Trending Restaurants lists update weekly, Apple says you’ll want to save any places you plan to visit. There’s a convenient + button next to each listing.

It’s unclear exactly how many different parts of the US have localized lists in iOS 27. But if you poke around and find the full collection of Local Lists, there are 1,021 total—so you’ll probably have one in your area.

You can browse all available lists by opening a Trending Restaurants list then tapping where you see the Apple logo and ‘Local Lists’ near the text that says when it was last updated.

Have you used Local Lists in iOS 27’s Maps app yet? Let us know what you think via the comments.

Scoop, suction, and flush clogged gutters safely with both feet on the ground

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Few home maintenance chores feel more daunting than clearing clogged gutters. Dragging an extension ladder across uneven flowerbeds, leaning precariously over shrubs, and scooping wet sludge by hand is both exhausting and genuinely dangerous.

Ignoring the buildup is not an option either, as overflowing gutters quickly send rainwater pouring down your siding and pooling against your foundation. The trick to clearing your roofline safely comes down to extending your reach from the ground, removing loose debris before you add water, and knowing when a clog is too stubborn for a pole attachment.

As damp leaves and pine needles pack together, they form a heavy dam that blocks rainwater from reaching the downspouts. That trapped water spills over the lip of the trough, soaking fascia boards until the wood rots and saturating the soil around your foundation walls, where leaks and basement dampness soon follow.

In colder months, standing water inside a blocked gutter also freezes solid, adding enough weight to pull brackets loose from the roofline or form damaging ice dams under your shingles.

Here are three simple ways to clear your gutters cleanly while keeping both feet firmly on the ground.

Blasting leaves out with a leaf blower works over open grass, yet it creates a mess over decks, patio furniture, or flowerbeds. A gutter attachment kit for a standard wet/dry shop vac keeps that debris contained while letting you work safely from the lawn.

Brands like Craftsman sell these universal kits at hardware stores and Amazon. Each kit includes three or four rigid plastic extension wands that click together into a 10-to-14-foot pole, topped with a curved, U-shaped nozzle.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Hold the assembled pole like a pool skimmer, hook the curved nozzle over the gutter lip, and switch the vacuum on to pull dry leaves, twigs, and grit straight down into the canister beside you.

Work in short sections along the wall, lifting the hook over each gutter bracket as you walk, and wear eye protection and gloves in case stray debris drops from above.

This four-piece accessory kit fits Craftsman and most other wet/dry vacs with a 2-1/2-inch hose, giving you two rigid extension wands, a curved gutter nozzle for suction, and a blower nozzle to clear dry leaves safely from the ground.

If your debris is too damp for a vacuum to lift, grabbing a hose right away will only turn the leaves into heavy, wet paste.

Instead, attach a curved gutter scoop or stiff brush to a telescopic extension pole suited to your roofline height. Work in short sections and focus on lifting material up and out of the channel rather than pushing it toward the downspout, which only packs debris tighter into the outlet.

If you cannot see over the lip of the trough, clipping a small pole-mounted inspection camera to the shaft lets you spot any leftover buildup without guessing.

Once you have removed the bulk of the leaves, you still need to clear fine shingle grit and confirm that water can actually escape down the pipe.

Hook a curved garden-hose attachment over the gutter lip and run a gentle stream of water rather than a high-pressure blast, which can loosen gutter brackets or force water up under your shingles. Work toward the downspout to wash remaining dirt away.

If water starts backing up over the edge, turn the hose off immediately rather than adding more water, as a persistent blockage inside the downspout elbow usually needs to be cleared by hand.

Extension poles and vacuum kits handle routine single-story maintenance easily, yet they have clear limits. If your roofline sits beyond a standard 24-foot reach, never stand on a chair or makeshift platform to bridge the gap.

Ground tools also struggle with years of packed mud, heavy branches, or thick mats of wet pine needles. Skip the DIY approach and call a professional if you face severe clogs, overhead power lines near the roof, interior water leaks, or gutters pulling loose from the fascia board.

#3162. IEEE Program Schools Preuniversity Educators On Tech Topics

The TryEngineering workshops help teachers deliver engaging STEM lessons

An educator constructs a microchip model during the IEEE Making a Microchip lesson plan demonstration.

Now in their third year, the IEEE TryEngineering educator sessions continue to empower preuniversity teachers with specialized professional development programs on engineering topics and classroom-tested lessons.

This year’s sessions, held across the United States, have focused on educating teachers about artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology. One session was held in Egypt.

In all, 54 educators learned about the engineering design process this year. They received an overview of TryEngineering resources including the Making of a Microchip and Train Your Tree lesson plans.

Workshops are scheduled this year in Greece and Guatemala.

The TryEngineering program is administered by IEEE Educational Activities.

These teachers and guest speakers attended the two-day session held at the Florida Semiconductor Institute and SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.IEEE Educational Activities

Central to the educator session program’s success is its university network. Host campuses welcome teachers into their facilities, where faculty provide background information about some of the technologies being taught, as well as possible engineering career paths and job opportunities for students.

This year’s sessions involved the educators in hands-on projects. Facilitators at each location were selected based on their experience in engineering education, and they worked with the TryEngineering staff on their presentations.

Sixteen teachers from nine schools participated in the session, held in Cairo. It was facilitated by Marwa Soudi, an IEEE member, and Senior Member Stamatis Dragoumanos. Both are past chairs of the IEEE preuniversity coordinating committee. GEMS provided outstanding STEM facilities for teachers, Saudi and Dragoumanos said. Participants received an overview of the Working With Wind Energy and Tall Tower Challenge lesson plans.

Another educator session is scheduled for later this year.

Educators from across the state gathered at the university’s Florida Semiconductor Institute, headquartered in Gainesville, and FSI’s NeoCity high-tech manufacturing campus near Orlando. The session was hosted by Roseanne Perez, an FSI workforce development program specialist, and Sophia Watson, FSI’s assistant director of workforce development. The two-day experience featured an inside look at microelectronics through a guided tour of a SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.

Engineering instructor Mary Acken facilitated hands-on lesson demonstrations for the 15 attending teachers.

Reflecting on the workshop’s impact, one participant said the SkyWater tour was excellent, the instructors were great, and the teachers enjoyed learning from like-minded educators.

Michael Kozicki, an IEEE member, and Stefan Myhajlenko from the university’s engineering school welcomed 11 Arizona teachers to the Tempe campus.

The session was facilitated by Janet Hartkopf, an Arizona school leader and a former TryEngineering educator session participant. Hartkopf highlighted collaborative learning, the need for diverse perspectives in engineering education, and career paths.

The teachers received instruction on how to implement the hands-on lessons in their classrooms, and they toured the university’s NanoFab facility to observe microelectronics research.

“This training was amazing!” said a participant who leads an elementary after-school STEM club. “I loved the hands-on lessons and e-books, which I will definitely be using with my students. I am excited to explore all the resources on the TryEngineering website. The experts from ASU were great.”

Sixteen STEM educators attended this session, held at the university’s International Institute for Biosensing in Minneapolis. Its director, Patricia Khashayar, an IEEE member, introduced participants to the capabilities of the university’s Supercomputing Institute and Nano Center.

Under the guidance of Claire Dietz, an education and outreach coordinator, and Pam Schumacher, an instructor at St. Paul College, the teachers completed classroom-ready lessons including a photonics experiment using the Nano Center’s equipment. Schumacher attended last year’s TryEngineering educator session.

Nano Center Director Sarah Swisher, an IEEE senior member, provided an overview of semiconductor operations and highlighted growing job opportunities for the state’s young people.

The experience inspired all 16 teachers to plan student field trips to the Nano Center during the upcoming academic year, they said.

“Great class!” one participant said. “I’m excited to bring some of the TryEngineering materials back to our school.”

This year’s sessions built on the momentum from last year when, with financial support from Onsemi’s Giving Now program, nearly 80 teachers attended sessions across five U.S. states and Mexico.

Driven by that success and the demand for more, the IEEE Educational Activities Board continued its support. Upcoming global sessions are expected to expand the program’s international footprint.

“I appreciated the time to collaborate with peers on how to implement hands-on lessons,” one participating teacher this year said. Some participants said they planned follow-up visits with the experts and campus tours.

You can learn more about the sessions by emailing TryEngineering.

Debra Gulick is director of IEEE student and academic educational programs.

#3161. Microsoft restores Outlook and Teams after two-day global outage

Microsoft outage disrupts Outlook, Teams and Copilot worldwide, with Claude and ChatGPT integrations also affected

Microsoft logo at the Microsoft Experience Center, New York

Microsoft said on Saturday that it had restored service to its remaining customers and regions, about two days after the outage began, the Associated Press reported.

The company said the problem was caused by an issue during an earlier upgrade to its network capacity, which surfaced after a recent network change. It again said there was no sign of malicious activity, and said on Friday that the outage was not caused by AI agents.

Separately, US officials said the outage was not linked to Friday’s nationwide flight ground stop.

A global Microsoft outage has disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services for more than 12 hours, affecting businesses, government agencies, financial institutions and airlines across several continents.

The disruption has also spread to third-party AI services, with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude reporting problems with their Microsoft 365 connectors.

The trouble began on Thursday in the Americas and spread globally within an hour. Outage reports reached 74 countries and territories in that time, according to Downdetector, which recorded a tenfold jump in UK reports at 17:43 UTC, followed by surges in India and New Zealand as their workdays began.

Microsoft has ruled out a cyberattack. Charles Lamanna, the company’s executive vice president for Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X that there was no indication the disruption resulted from malicious or cyber activity.

@MSFT365Status We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue. We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.

— Charles Lamanna (@clamanna) November 13, 2026

However, restoring services has proved more difficult than initially expected. After reporting positive results from its recovery measures, Microsoft said overnight that traffic rerouting and strategic blocking were delivering only partial improvements, rather than sustained recovery.

The company has continued restarting affected servers and applying additional mitigation measures, but some changes have not worked as expected.

The outage has had consequences well beyond Microsoft’s own products. Bankers at Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs in Hong Kong told CNN they had been unable to access email and Teams throughout the day.

Japan’s government returned to paper-based processes after ministries struggled to send emails for much of Friday. Australia’s spy agency and federal police were also among the affected organisations.

The Philippine Supreme Court warned of delays, while Australian schools and courts reported email disruptions. US city governments, including Miami Beach and Austin, asked residents to use phone services instead. A Colorado sheriff’s office said the outage had delayed bond payments for prisoners.

Airlines including IndiGo and Akasa lost email support channels, while electric vehicle maker Workhorse postponed its earnings call because of business disruptions. Financial institutions, including Standard Chartered and ING Australia, also warned customers about scammers impersonating technical support staff and attempting to exploit the disruption.

The disruption has extended to AI services that rely on Microsoft’s productivity infrastructure. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported problems with their Microsoft 365 connectors, which allow their AI assistants to access workplace information such as emails, calendars, Teams conversations and SharePoint files.

OpenAI said it was investigating elevated errors affecting its Microsoft 365 connector. The company warned that new connections could fail and that existing tools might not work as expected.

Anthropic reported similar problems with Claude’s Microsoft 365 connector. Mail, calendar and search requests were failing for most users, while some users were also unable to open Claude for Outlook or use its mail and calendar functions.

Anthropic traced the problem to an upstream provider and subsequently confirmed that it was caused by the Microsoft 365 service incident.

The disruption does not mean that ChatGPT or Claude are entirely offline. The problems concern their connections to Microsoft’s services, rather than their underlying AI models. Anthropic’s status page lists the Claude API and Claude Code as operational, although Claude.ai and Claude Cowork have also been reporting degraded performance.

The incidents illustrate how an outage affecting a major productivity platform can spread to third-party applications and AI assistants that depend on its infrastructure.

The likely cause of the disruption remains under investigation. Australia’s home affairs minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believed it was dealing with something similar to the CrowdStrike incident in 2024, describing it as an update that had gone wrong, according to CNN.

Microsoft has not confirmed that explanation as the root cause, and its investigation has focused on affected servers and recent configuration changes, while its recovery efforts have centred on restoring capacity and stabilising the infrastructure.

The timing is particularly pointed for Europe, where the outage coincided with EU leaders meeting in Dublin to discuss reducing the continent’s dependence on foreign technology providers.

The 2024 CrowdStrike incident exposed the risks of relying on a small number of technology providers for critical services. The latest Microsoft disruption adds another example of how problems at a single infrastructure provider can affect organisations across industries and countries, including services built by other technology companies.

For businesses relying on Microsoft 365, the incident also raises questions about contingency planning. When email, calendars and workplace collaboration tools become unavailable, organisations can quickly lose access to the systems they depend on to communicate with customers, employees and partners.

As Microsoft’s recovery efforts continue, the outage is a reminder that cloud-based productivity services are interconnected, and that a failure in one part of the ecosystem can have consequences far beyond the company experiencing the technical problem.

#3160. This tiny iOS 27 camera feature really makes a huge difference

When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.

But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so …

Developers know that a big reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app.

Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap.

Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure.

It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video).

Of course, third-party apps still have an important role, but this one change has made a big difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video.

Do you make use of this feature yourself? If so, please share the details in the comments.

#3159. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA

The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

“I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”

Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA

Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA

MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

From that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA

It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR

“It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR

Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR

The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says.

Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy

Idefix’s interactions with its new home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel says the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”

Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA

During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

“We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

“MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

Andrew Jones is a freelance journalist based near Helsinki. He writes about the space industry and technology with a particular focus on China's activities.

#3158. Stop doing sit-ups — a yoga instructor and strength and conditioning coach recommends this exercise to work the core, hip flexors, and back muscles

This move helps build stability rather than just endurance

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Did you know that when it comes to building core strength and stability, sit-ups and crunches aren’t the best place to start? Unless you perform them with perfect form, sit-ups and crunches can stress your lower back and neck because you repeatedly bend your spine forward under load.

What’s more, if, like me, you’re a runner or spend a lot of time sitting behind a desk, there’s a high chance your hip flexors take over during this move. This can pull on your lower back, causing discomfort.

Instead, yoga instructor and strength and conditioning coach Melissa Leach recommends a simple yoga pose to build deep core strength and spinal stability. Read on to find out more.

As a reminder, if you’re a complete beginner, pregnant or postpartum, or returning to fitness following an injury or surgery, this might not be the right move for you and your body. It’s always best to seek personalized advice from a qualified professional.

The move Leach recommends over sit-ups and crunches is the boat pose. "Boat pose is one of the most efficient core exercises because it doesn't just isolate the abs; it engages the hip flexors, glutes, pelvic muscles, and back all at once, helping build functional core strength rather than working one single muscle in isolation,” she says.

All you’ll need is your bodyweight, but using one of the best yoga mats can help make things more comfortable.

“There are different ways to perform boat pose. Traditional holds usually consist of staying in the pose for a total of 25 breaths, broken into five sets, while others add movement by hinging the upper body upward and downward,” says Leach. “This version is a more accessible entry point for beginners, starting with bent knees and shorter, more manageable holds.”

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

“For beginners, keeping your legs bent in a half boat pose instead of straight can help reduce the core strain and effort required at the start. Lightly gripping the backs of your thighs can also provide support to help you balance,” says Leach.

“If you struggle with balance and maintaining a straight spine, you can either sit on a folded blanket or cushion to help tilt the pelvis forward, or sit with your back a few inches from the wall for reassurance.

“The most important thing is to get a hold of the technique first, so start slowly, only holding for as long as it's comfortable and slowly increasing the length as your core strength improves.”

On paper, this move looks simple, but after 20 seconds, you’ll know it’s anything but. Holding your torso and legs lifted activates your rectus abdominis (six-pack muscles), obliques, and deeper transverse abdominis at the same time. You’ll also work the muscles along your spine, counteracting bad posture from prolonged sitting.

As you hold your legs off the floor, you’ll work your hip flexors, quadriceps, and inner thighs, as well as working your balance and coordination.

"Boat pose also helps build stability rather than just endurance. Holding the position forces your deep core muscles, the ones that support your spine and pelvis, to switch on and stay engaged throughout. Over time, this can translate into better posture, a stronger lower back, and a core that supports your everyday movement," Leach adds.

Once your boat hold feels comfortable, one of the easiest ways to increase the intensity is to hold the pose longer or simply raise both arms straight up alongside your ears. This increases the demand on your core.

Alternatively, you can also add a pulse. To do this, start in boat pose and slowly lower your torso and straight legs towards the floor, then pull back up into full boat. Move slowly and with complete control.

#3156. Italy fines Meta €805m over Facebook’s access to Android photos

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg at a dinner with tech leaders in the State Dining Room of the White House in Washington, Sept. 4, 2025.

Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805m, or about $887m. It says the Facebook app for Android accessed photos, videos and their metadata on Italian users’ phones without specific consent or proper notice.

The decision, first reported in English by Reuters, targets a gallery suggestions feature available since 2023. While users scroll Facebook, it offers photos and videos from their phone as ideas for posts.

The Garante found that Facebook asked for gallery access with one permission for the whole app. That request followed a vague prompt to enable other features. Users could not tell they were also switching on gallery suggestions.

The regulator said about 20 million Android users in Italy were affected. It also weighed a 2019 decision against Meta and what it called poor cooperation. Changes Meta made after the complaint counted in its favour, but the Garante called them late and limited to users who update the app.

The fine equals about 0.47% of Meta’s global turnover. Within 60 days, Meta must ask for separate, specific consent for the feature. It must also keep the feature off by default, even for users who already granted access.

The probe did not examine whether gallery content was used to train AI, which Meta denies. The Garante will look separately at a cloud processing feature launched in 2026.

The penalty is close to the €825m Dutch fine on Uber, though below Meta’s €1.2bn GDPR fine over data transfers. Meta is also tangling with Italy over a ruling on publisher payments.

Reuters said Meta was not immediately available for comment.

#3155. How to Check Your Flight Status After the FAA Canceled the Ground Stop for All Airports

Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration announced it has ended the ground stop.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

At this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't said what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for users of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

This is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

#3154. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3153. iOS 27.3 adds three new features I’ve used almost every day

iOS 27.3 is coming next month, and during the beta so far there are three new features I’ve been using almost every day.

Siri AI in iOS 27 brings major upgrades by providing world knowledge, personal context features, and being more conversational than ever. But one previously announced Siri improvement—an expanded set of actions for Apple apps—didn’t make the cut in iOS 27.0.

Now in iOS 27.3, though, Apple is rolling out its first set of new app actions for Siri AI.

Siri AI has new capabilities across apps like Calendar, Files, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It’s a big step toward making voice-driven computing more powerful on Apple platforms, and I’ve had fun experimenting with everything new Siri can do.

Read more: iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

Apple Health gets a big overhaul in iOS 27.3, with a fresh design and new features that utilize Apple Intelligence for more personalized health insights. Per Apple:

The updated experience includes a new Insights tab that surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.

In my testing so far, I’ve especially enjoyed getting up-to-date guidance every day on my health metrics, browsing the deep collection of new educational videos and articles, and understanding all the factors that contribute to longevity. I think Apple is moving the right direction with this update.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, iOS 27.3 adds a powerful new feature called Siri Recap that “ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory.”

"iOS 27.3 adds three new features I've used almost every day", "Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving". What's with these terrible clickbait titles lately? Did we go back to 2014?

Siri Recap functions like an outsourced short-term memory reserve. The data it collects is saved inside the Siri app in a new Recaps tab, where it lives for seven days and is then deleted—unless you manually save a specific recap.

So far in the beta, I’ve found the summaries Siri generates to strike a good balance of being helpful but not too invasive. It reminds me of key details, but there’s nothing I’ve seen that feels overly sensitive or personalized. That may change over time the more I use it, but so far I think this could prove a really valuable feature.

#3152. Perplexity brings AI agents feature called Teammates to the Mac

This week, Perplexity has deployed its new proactive agentic AI feature called Teammates to the Mac. Perplexity Teammates were previously limited to iOS and the web.

Similar to Grok Bot, Perplexity Teammates are task-oriented proactive agentic AI threads that work for you without constantly being prompted. Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots are similar, but use a single chat model rather than supporting multiple instances.

Teammates are a team of AI agents that own ongoing work. Give a teammate a responsibility, such as managing a growth campaign, triaging incoming bug reports, tracking your metrics, or researching a new market, and it owns that work around the clock. It plans the tasks, brings in more agents when the work grows, and follows through until the result is ready for your review.

Access to Teammates currently requires a paid Perplexity Max subscription. The feature builds on top of Perplexity’s existing AI orchestration system.

#3151. Jensen Huang struggled to reach Beijing’s chip policymakers, FT says

Nvidia had no dedicated China government team until late 2025, and Beijing’s security camp won the argument over its chips.

NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang during his GTC 2026 keynote at the SAP Center in San Jose, 16 March 2026

Jensen Huang spent years courting China, but he struggled to reach the officials who decided Nvidia’s fate there, the Financial Times reported. The paper cited people familiar with the matter.

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday. He had admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials suspect of spying for China. Beijing denies she is a spy, and the two are not related.

The FT looks at what came before. Huang visited China six times in three years. His first recorded meeting with a top leader came in April 2025, with Vice-Premier He Lifeng. In July 2025 he met He again, and commerce minister Wang Wentao too.

Those meetings ran through Ren Hongbin, who heads China’s main trade promotion body, the FT said. But Nvidia never secured talks with the National Development and Reform Commission. The FT says the state planner led Beijing’s push to restrict Nvidia chips.

Huang also failed to win more time with Wang once those curbs arrived. Part of the problem was Nvidia’s thin lobbying, the FT said. It had no dedicated team for Chinese officials until late 2025, when it hired Tony Jiang from Intel.

Beijing was also split, according to the paper. The commerce ministry saw Nvidia chips as a bridge while Huawei caught up. Security officials saw reliance on Nvidia as a weakness, and their view has gained ground over the past year.

Huang often warned Washington that export curbs would only help Huawei. Now some say his exit will do the same.

“It may sound ironic, but the fall of Jensen helps to strengthen Huawei’s leading position in China,” George Chen, a partner at the Asia Group, told the FT.

In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump’s business delegation to China. He briefly spoke with Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang, the most senior leaders he had met in public.

Nvidia, the commerce ministry and China’s cyberspace regulator did not respond to the FT. Nvidia’s board inquiry continues, and it reports third-quarter results on 17 November.

My favorite thing about this robot vacuum is the extended reach. Most standard vacuums try their best to get ot the edges of the room, but almost always miss the corners. Speaking of getting into small spaces, the sensor on top of the vacuum is retractable. This means that it can easily get under low furniture up to 3.54 inches high. During testing, it easily made its way under my low-lying sofa, and the LED lighting came on to guide the way.

The retractable legs are the real star of the show here. They help the robot make its way over small ledges, high-pile carpets, and even obstacles like table legs. It's a very helpful assistant to have in the house and makes cleanup after a busy day much easier.

You can find out more about the robot vacuum by reading my full Dreame X50 Ultra Complete review.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.
