#3119. MacBook Neo 2: Here’s everything we know so far

Apple released the all-new MacBook Neo earlier this year, and it’s been a resounding success by all indications. Here’s everything we know so far about what’s next for Apple’s most affordable laptop …

The current MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip, which is the same chip used in the iPhone 16 Pro. As reported by Bloomberg, Apple is working on a next-generation MacBook Neo powered by the A19 Pro chip.

In terms of performance, the A19 Pro is about 10-15% faster than the A18 Pro in single-core and multi-core CPU tests. The jump in GPU performance is even bigger, with benchmarks showing an up to 40% boost for the A19 Pro. This is because every GPU core in the A19 Pro has Neural Accelerators built in.

The A19 Pro chip is also used in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone Air.

According to reporter Tim Culpan, Apple will likely use a “binned” version of the A19 Pro chip in the MacBook Neo. While the A19 Pro chip in the iPhone 17 Pro has a 6-core GPU, the MacBook Neo version of the chip will likely have a 5-core GPU.

One of the compromises of the MacBook Neo is that it has 8GB of RAM. The rest of Apple’s Mac lineup nowadays starts with 16GB of RAM.

The next-generation MacBook Neo won’t jump all the way to 16GB of RAM. Instead, it’s expected to offer 12GB of RAM thanks to the aforementioned A19 Pro.

As I wrote in my review, I don’t think it’s a huge limitation that the MacBook Neo has just 8GB of RAM. Still, an increase for the next-generation model is a great improvement.

The combination of the A19 Pro chip and 12GB of RAM upgrades should also unlock support for Apple’s more powerful on-device AI model announced at WWDC. This model enables a more accurate dictation experience and new options for customizing the Siri voice.

The current MacBook Neo doesn’t support this feature because of its A18 Pro chip and 8GB of RAM.

The MacBook Neo is available in an array of fun colors, including citrus, blush, indigo, and silver. Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plan is to “periodically” update the MacBook Neo with new colors.

There aren’t any details on which colors the next-generation MacBook Neo will be available in.

Apple released the current MacBook Neo in March. Tim Culpan reports that the A19 Pro version of the machine is slated for a release sometime in 2027.

#3118. Why Fervo Energy Stock Surged This Week

The company's signing of an agreement with an industry powerhouse led to fervent investor enthusiasm for Fervo stock.

A landmark 15-year power purchase agreement with Alphabet (GOOGL -0.98%) (GOOG -0.96%) and operational progress at its Utah facility sent Fervo Energy (FRVO -1.20%) soaring 297% this week, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence.

Fervo Energy stock closed at $11.51 on Friday, Nov. 13, up 29% from its close on Friday, Nov. 6. Over the same period, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.40%) gained 2.5%, and the Nasdaq-100 was up 3.5%.

Fervo Energy reported third-quarter 2026 results on Monday, Nov. 9, revealing that its contracted revenue backlog expanded to $11.9 billion, up from $7.2 billion in the prior quarter. The surge was anchored by a 15-year deal to supply 396 megawatts of geothermal electricity to Google, which management described as the largest enhanced geothermal power purchase agreement signed to date. Operational progress supported the financial numbers, as the company's first 33-megawatt GeoBlock at its Cape Station site in Utah entered commercial operation on Sept. 30, 2026, followed by grid synchronization of a second block on Nov. 4, 2026.

Fervo Energy is a pre-revenue geothermal developer building enhanced geothermal power plants. With minimal commercial revenue yet, its value depends on whether its Utah project scales as planned. Enhanced geothermal technology uses horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing techniques adapted from the oil industry to harvest heat from deep subterranean rock formations. The developer sells clean, continuous electricity directly to utility grids and corporate customers seeking carbon-free power, meeting demand from energy-intensive data centers.

The stock remains down 73% from its 52-week high, reflecting heavy selling following its May initial public offering and recent short-seller scrutiny. This week's Google deal expansion resolves early doubts about commercial viability, shifting the thesis from proving enhanced geothermal technology to executing multi-gigawatt project builds.

Management expects capital expenditures for the second half of 2026 to land between $700 million and $750 million as construction accelerates across the 8.4-gigawatt Cape Station resource. Fervo Energy ended last quarter with $1.9 billion in cash and short-term investments as of Sept. 30, 2026, against a $19.5 million quarterly net loss, giving it cash runway to fund ongoing drilling without immediate equity dilution. It's difficult to apply a strict multiple-comparison approach here because pre-revenue renewable utilities trade on project funding, regulatory approvals, and power agreement backlogs rather than earnings multiples.

Because Fervo Energy has no commercial revenue, the risk of permanent capital loss remains high if subterranean reservoirs fail to maintain operational temperatures over time or if project execution delays trigger costly contract penalties. Investors should watch for further updates on Cape Station Phase I commercial deliveries and management's scheduled year-end operational update.

While nuclear energy receives the lion's share of investors' attention as a potential solution to the massive power demands of data centers, geothermal is stealing some of the spotlight thanks to Fervo's new agreement with Google. Plus, the $12 billion backlog that Fervo reported represents another bright green flag.

Potential investors, however, must recognize that, despite the recent development, this renewable energy stock is best left for those comfortable with a more speculative investment, as the company is still not generating revenue. For those with higher risk tolerances considering positions, monitoring the company's progress on Cape Station GeoBlock 1 in the coming quarters is essential to confirm that its growth remains on track.

Some people visit a Starbucks or LEGO store everywhere they travel. I go to Gentle Monster.

The Korean eyewear brand’s stores are a regular stop on my itineraries, partly to pick up a pair of sunglasses, but mostly to see what wonderfully strange art installation awaits inside. So when Gentle Monster invited me to try its new Google-powered Intelligent Eyewear at a New York City pop-up, I expected something totally unconventional.

What I, perhaps, didn’t expect? That I’d be asking Gemini to interpret a tarot pull while contemplating my wedding planning alongside realistic horse animatronics, a ginormous fuzzy blue monster and a bulletin of Bermuda Triangle conspiracy theories.

Founded in Seoul in 2011, Gentle Monster’s identity is built on experimental eyewear and avant-garde retail design. Its fashion credentials include collaborations with Moncler and Maison Margiela, but teaming up with Google is a new frontier of style and technology.

What kind of relationship should technology have with humanity?

The intricacies of such a relationship is on full display at the pop-up space timed to the release of Google Intelligent Eyewear collections, starting at $449 for Gentle Monster styles. The Wall Street warehouse has been transformed into a multi-environment experience intended to learn through Gemini on the smart glasses.

Inside the pop-up, I sat down in front of a tarot deck, unfamiliar with where to start. I asked Gemini to walk me through pulling a reading, step-by-step, starting with intense focus on a pointed question a while I shuffled. I’m planning a wedding, so uncertainty and anxiety around budgeting is hardly in short supply.

I then learned how to pick my cards, and how they could be interpreted based on the order in which I pulled them. Naturally, I took Gemini’s explanations with a grain of salt, but appreciated having a way into something unfamiliar without needing to know the right questions first.

I spotted gochujang and asked for an easy recipe using ingredients I probably already had at home, and Gemini suggested a delicious-sounding noodle dish.

In a gym setting, I asked it to walk me through throwing a football with a proper spiral. A museum-style display about Bermuda Triangle conspiracies offered another rabbit hole, with material in different languages for Gemini to help explain.

Most memorably, I spoke English with a woman speaking Mandarin about her hometown of Shenzhen. After a few exchanges, the translation’s slight delay became less distracting, and I could follow my curiosity about the city’s traditional food culture.

Then there was the massive showroom installation featuring faceless, crawling AI mannequins alongside hyper-realistic horse animatronics assembled by hand.

Gentle Monster says the collection began with a question: “What kind of relationship should technology have with humanity?” Its answer positions technology as something that can expand how we perceive and experience the world.

I appreciated Gentle Monster’s commitment to physical art in the wake of introducing yet another way to bring AI into our lives, and now literally on our faces. There’s remarkable human craftsmanship to examine, and doing so while wearing Google intelligent eyewear only elevated my ability to appreciate the abundance of creativity it takes to design a space like this.

That’s what keeps me visiting Gentle Monster stores around the world. The spaces always reward curiosity. Here, the glasses gave me another way to act on it, whether I was navigating a language barrier or admitting I didn’t know how to read tarot cards

#3115. Jensen Huang is discussing a return to Nvidia, FT reports

Two big Nvidia investors want the board to keep the door open. The Treasury Secretary wants an outsider instead.

Jensen Huang at Nvidia’s GTC Berlin keynote, 21 October 2026.

Jensen Huang has been discussing a possible comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, days after the board pushed him out, the Financial Times reported. Bloomberg relayed the report on Sunday.

Huang resigned on Thursday. He had admitted an affair with Alice Huang, whom US officials suspect of spying for China, and was reported to have had another with an Nvidia vice president. The two Huangs are not related, and Beijing denies the spying claims.

Several Silicon Valley allies have begun lobbying for his return, the FT said. Two of them are Nvidia investors. In a letter to the board posted on X, Altimeter’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides’ Gavin Baker urged a slow and deliberate approach to choosing a successor.

That approach should include “the potential return of Jensen Huang,” they wrote.

Washington is pulling the other way. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News that Nvidia needs a dramatic shakeup in its leadership. He said it should look outside the company for its next chief.

Bessent has made the scandal about chips, not private life. On Friday he said anyone at Nvidia should be held accountable if its chips leaked to China.

A return would also have to survive the board’s own inquiry, which is run by Wachtell Lipton. Huang is expected to testify before Congress, and Nvidia reports results on Tuesday under interim chief executive Colette Kress.

#3114. Investors: If a Market Correction Is Coming, This 1 Move Will Make or Break Your Portfolio

When investing in individual stocks, one thing matters above all else if you want to minimize the pain of drawdowns.

The stock market has begun to tumble — especially the technology stocks associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out. In fact, the Nasdaq-100 index has already entered a correction, down over 11% from its highs.

Could the S&P 500 index follow suit? Market corrections are normal, and investors should expect them to occur on a regular basis. However, in order to mitigate the pain of market drawdowns, investors who buy individual stocks should utilize this one strategy.

Diversification is the practice of keeping your savings in different baskets so that if one idea falls apart, you are not going to lose everything.

Most portfolios should have a minimum of 20-30 stocks to benefit from diversification. The Motley Fool recommends 50. There is some nuance to this: An investor with just $1,000 in savings should not feel the need to put it into 50 stocks. Wait until you have more in the bank account to slowly build out this portfolio.

Someone with six figures or seven figures in savings could definitely spread their savings over 50 or so stocks in order to stay properly diversified. That way, if one of the stocks you own goes to zero, the rest can pick up the slack.

Fifty stocks for an individual investor is a good sweet spot. Much more, and the portfolio can feel too crowded and overwhelming to manage. Much less, and you are exposed to massive amounts of volatility, which you may or may not want to experience.

Of course, there is even more nuance to building a portfolio than there is in having 50 stocks. One needs to consider what sectors to spread their bets around. If 40 of the 50 stocks you own are centered in a risky sector like AI, you may have significantly less diversification than you think.

Or, there is the risk of having one or two positions be massive in your portfolio. If the majority of your portfolio was Nvidia and Micron Technology this year, it wouldn't matter how many other stocks you own; they would be too insignificant to replace the massive drawdowns from these two AI infrastructure stocks.

Investors can also consider diversifying into different stock sizes, factors, and geographies, which tend to have uncorrelated performance. Factors can be complicated, but the most popular are value stocks, which are the statistically cheapest stocks on the market. Match them with some AI technology stocks, and your portfolio is starting to diversify quite quickly.

All you need to do is look at your own portfolio. If you have too much of your portfolio in one or two stocks, or in a single sector, now would be a great time to spread some of your eggs into different baskets. This could span different stock sectors, high-dividend payers, small-cap value stocks, new geographies, or even non-stock assets like bonds and real estate.

Owning bonds and real estate can be uncorrelated to short-term stock market performance. This is why the 60/40 portfolio exists: It allows you to rebalance the uncorrelated returns from bonds and buy stocks on the cheap during a market correction, another form of diversification outside of just owning many different stocks.

Everyone will have their own preferences. At the end of the day, if you don't put all your eggs in one basket and avoid using leverage by trading on margin, you will do just fine through a market correction.

#3113. Hands-on: This 25W MagSafe charger is thinner than an iPhone: KUXIU K4 Air [Video]

When it comes to 3-in-1 travel chargers, I look at two main things: How fast it can charge my iPhone and how portable it is. I have tested plenty of travel chargers that aim to be as portable as possible by using lightweight materials or folding into a smaller footprint, but there usually seems to be some sort of compromise. But this new K4 Air by Kuxiu might be the most impressive option I’ve tested to date. This charger is just 8.5mm thin, weighs less than 120 g, and can wirelessly charge your iPhone at up to 25W. After spending a few weeks with it and traveling across the Atlantic, here is what you should know about the Kuxiu K4 Air.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video with the K4 Air to see it in action!

The biggest selling point of the new Kuxiu K4 Air is its design. When completely folded, this thing is barely thicker than an iPhone. For reference, my iPhone 17 Pro measures roughly 8.25mm thick, while the K4 Air comes in at just 8.5mm. That is insanely compact for something that can charge three devices at once. And even though they went ultra-slim, they did not really need to sacrifice any charging performance. You get:

One of my favorite things about Kuxiu has always been their price-to-performance ratio. While some brands and companies are removing charging bricks and even cables, Kuxiu is adding a ton of value here by including everything you need directly in the packaging. The build quality of the charger is also fantastic. It feels balanced, well-made, and extremely versatile because of all the situations you can use it in.

Kuxiu has also done a great job of bringing us a Burgundy color option that perfectly matches the new Burgundy iPhone color. I wish Apple would continue making the Cosmic Orange iPhone because the K4 Air in that orange would have been awesome.

I recommend watching our video to see my reaction when I pick up the K4 Air for the first time. I was shocked at how small it was. It was thin and lightweight, but still felt solid because it was made of metal and not plastic. The form factor and size make it incredibly easy to throw into any bag, pocket, purse, or even just leave it attached to your iPhone for when it is needed.

The charging experience is actually pretty straightforward. You unfold the charger, connect the USB-C cable, and you’re ready to go. The main magnetic charging surface supports your iPhone, while the second surface is for AirPods. They even added magnets to the AirPods charging pad to ensure they stay in place every single time. There is also a dedicated Apple Watch charger that folds down to charge any Apple Watch. I was charging my Apple Watch Ultra 4, and it fit perfectly.

But now the big question: how well does it work with the iPhone Duo? Personally, I charge my iPhone Duo on my nightstand charger when it is folded shut. So I have zero issues with it. But if you open the iPhone, place it on the charger in landscape mode, and then use it, it will tilt slightly to the left. But to my surprise, if you use the iPhone Duo and open it in portrait mode, it works great! The charger doubles as a stand and easily supports the iPhone Duo. Another cool piece that the form factor unlocks is that it can technically charge two iPhones at the same time, so if you are in a pinch, you can charge two iPhones at once,

So, regardless of which iPhone you are using, as long as it supports MagSafe, you are good to go. But how much does something like this cost?

The Kuxiu K4 Air is finally back in stock after a limited initial run. You can get it on Kuxiu’s website for $79. It comes in Space Gray and their new Burgundy color. As I mentioned above, you also get the charging cable, a 45W charging brick, and a carrying pouch.

Personally, I am a huge fan of how good the Burgundy color looks.

After using the Kuxiu K4 Air, it is just one of those accessories that makes sense. It is small, compact, lightweight, and extremely useful. It fits perfectly into the travel charger category. There are a ton of great 3-in-1 chargers, with new ones flooding the market daily, but very few combine this level of portability with all the features we discussed.

So if you are shopping for a portable 3-in-1 travel charger for yourself or as a gift, I would highly recommend giving this one a shot. It’s well-built, charges your big three Apple products, and looks fantastic.

Whether you're planning to go away on a trip or stay home this holiday season, it's important that you keep an eye on everything in your house. From your chimney to your basement, front door to the back porch, you want to make sure every inch of your home is protected against any eventuality.

The best smart home devices can do just that. From smart thermostats to video doorbells to water leak detectors, these gadgets can let you know in a hurry if something's amiss, whether you're in the next room or the next state. Best of all, many are on sale for Black Friday.

This one is pretty obvious, but installing one of the best outdoor security cameras can let you see who's approaching your house from any angle. Some models also have built in floodlights and spotlights, which not only deters intruders, but can also help you if you're pulling into your driveway or walking up to your front door at night.

Inside, one of the best home security cameras not only can warn you if someone gets into your house, but can also be used to keep tabs on your pets while you're away. Since all cameras have built-in speakers, you could even shoo them off the couch if they're not supposed to sleep there.

This do-it-all outdoor security camera from Eufy has two lenses — a wide-angle and an 8X zoom — so you can get an expansive view of your yard, but then get close up to see something in more detail. Plus, the camera can pan and tilt, letting you track things more easily. And, the solar panel means you might never have to plug it in.

Looking for something a little cheaper? Blink's cameras offer excellent 2K resolution, and thanks to their innovative tech, can last up to two years without needing to replace their batteries. This deal gets you two cameras for 66% off.

This indoor/outdoor camera can pan 360º and tilt 115º, so it can track subjects as they move across your yard. It needs to be plugged in, but it has a 2K camera along with color night vision. It's a good inexpensive option, especially at half off.

The best video doorbells of course let you know who's knocking, but the models we like the most also have features such as package detection, so you know when UPS or FedEx has delivered something to your door. Thanks to AI, some video doorbells will even alert you if they see someone stealing a package, which is especially helpful around the holidays.

It's wild that one of the best video doorbells is so darn cheap. While not Ring's top-of-the-line model, you still get excellent 2K video and two-way talk, so you'll be able to see, hear and talk with anyone who may be lingering around your front door. At just $39, it's more than half off.

If you're heading out of town for the holidays and have a dog walker or sitter coming over, a smart lock is a super-helpful device. You can create custom codes for guests, and even create schedules for when they're allowed to get into your house — and when they're not. Plus, you'll get a notification on your phone any time someone unlocks your door.

Some of the more advanced smart locks also have fingerprint and palm readers, as well as the ability to be opened with an Apple Watch.

This smart lock is one of the first to have UWB technology, which means that it can unlock your door automatically when you approach it (with your phone). In our Aqara U400 review, it worked like magic. Apple owners will love it.

Is the turkey burning in the oven? A smart smoke detector will alert you to any smoke, fire, or carbon monoxide events in your home, so you can quickly act on any potential problems. Should you not want to replace all the alarms currently in your house, some of the best smart speakers can also listen for alarms and send you an alert, too.

This First Alert model is our top pick, as you can mix and match both battery-powered and interconnected alarms, which makes it the most versatile for new construction. It has a photoelectric and electrochemical detector, so it can pick up both fast-burning and smoldering fires, and it works with Google Home.

As we head into the winter months, the threat of freezing pipes becomes even more real. The last thing you want is to return home to a flooded basement. The best smart water leak detectors can alert you not just to when a leak is occurring, but also to temperature dips or rises in humidity levels, so you can act on a problem before it happens.

While we wish it had a louder alarm — and a longer battery life — we like that it works with Moen's automatic shutoff valve (should you have that installed) so that it can automatically turn off the water to your home if there's a major leak. You can get a pack of three for $139.

Smart plugs are cheap and easy ways to remotely control devices in your home. If you have floor or table lamps, plug them into a smart plug, and you can have them turn on and off at scheduled times, to make it look like you're home.

We like Tapo's smart plug for its ease of setup, and for the fact that it's Matter-compatible, which means it'll work with every major smart home platform — Amazon, Apple, Google, and SmartThings, among others.

One thing we have to worry about more during the winter is our power getting knocked out due to snow or ice storms. It's handy to have a battery backup on hand to keep your phone charged and the food in your fridge cold.

The Anker Solix S2000 has a 2,100Wh capacity, and can deliver 1,500W continuous and 3,000W peak power. Anker says it can power your refrigerator for up to 35 hours, too. All this in a compact 8.2 × 11.1 × 12.7 inch device that weighs only 35.7 pounds. And, you can recharge it using solar panels.

#3110. Which Short-Term Bond ETF Is the Better Buy: Vanguard’s Treasury Fund VGSH or Bond Fund BSV?

BSV offers higher yield but greater volatility, while VGSH provides pure Treasury exposure with lower drawdown risk. Both charge just 0.03% annually.

Vanguard Short-Term Bond ETF (BSV -0.04%) offers broader credit exposure and a higher yield, while Vanguard Short-Term Treasury ETF (VGSH +0.04%) provides a more conservative, pure-play Treasury portfolio for identical costs.

Both Vanguard Short-Term Treasury ETF and Vanguard Short-Term Bond ETF target the short end of the yield curve, providing investors with a way to manage cash while seeking stability. While they share the same ultra-low expense ratio, the primary difference lies in credit quality and diversification. VGSH sticks strictly to government debt, whereas BSV adds corporate and international bonds.

Beta measures price volatility relative to the S&P 500; beta is calculated from monthly returns over the available fund history (up to five years). The 1-yr return represents total return over the trailing 12 months. Dividend yield is the trailing-12-month distribution yield.

These funds are exceptionally affordable with identical 0.03% expense ratios. However, BSV provides a higher payout with its 4.5% yield, compared to the 4.1% offered by VGSH. This yield gap reflects the additional risk inherent in BSV's corporate bond holdings.

Vanguard Short-Term Bond ETF aims to mirror a float-adjusted index that includes investment-grade debt securities with maturities between one and five years. It is a fixed income fund with no equity sector breakdown, and its 3,155 holdings include the United States Treasury Note/Bond 4.38% 08/31/2031 at 1.70% and the United States Treasury Note/Bond 5.00% 09/30/2031 at 1.32%. This broader mandate allows it to capture credit spreads beyond Treasury yields. The fund was launched in 2007.

Vanguard Short-Term Treasury ETF employs a more concentrated strategy by tracking the Bloomberg US Treasury 1--3 Year Index. Like its peer, it is a fixed income fund with no equity sector breakdown. Its portfolio of 95 holdings includes the United States Treasury Note/Bond 3.50% 01/31/2028 at 2.07% and the United States Treasury Note/Bond 4.63% 04/30/2029 at 1.43%. Because it holds only government-backed debt, it generally offers lower price volatility than the bond fund. The fund was launched in 2009.

I'd go with VGSH, because the small bonus for owning corporate bonds instead of government bonds is not worth the extra risk right now. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates again in September, and companies are paying only a small bonus over the government to borrow, so reaching for credit risk is not rewarding you much right now.

VGSH owns only U.S. Treasuries, so there is no default risk, and its worst drop over five years was smaller than BSV's. Treasuries are also backed by the U.S. government, so they tend to hold up when markets get shaky. BSV yields a little more, but the difference is small, and over five years the two funds have grown almost the same amount.

BSV holds corporate and international bonds alongside Treasuries, which makes it a solid choice if you want a bit more income and can accept some credit risk. But for most long-term investors who want short-term bonds to be the calm part of a portfolio, VGSH is the better buy, and it costs exactly the same.

#3109. How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program offers ethics and compliance training

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3108. The new Apple TV has twice as much RAM as the previous model, but apps and games can’t use it

The new Apple TV 4K features an A19 chip inside with 128 GB storage and 8 GB RAM, twice the amount of memory as the previous version. Presumably, the supply crunch surrounding the memory chips is part of the reason this generation of Apple TV box jumped to a $299 price point as well.

However, although the specs have been upgraded, apps and games are not actually able to use more RAM for themselves. Apps on Apple TV are limited by the operating system to 2 GB RAM each, and that cap has not changed on the fourth-generation box.

Obviously, most of the apps you run on Apple TV are streaming service clients, which generally have much smaller RAM requirements anyway. However, ostensibly, Apple markets the Apple TV as a gaming device and RAM constraints matter much more there.

A hypothetically graphics-intensive game will easily hit the 2 GB RAM ceiling, and some fans had hoped that the new box with the new chip and double the internal memory would help here. Unfortunately, with the current tvOS software, that is not the case.

Apple really needs to remove these archaic restrictions, for the new overpriced model at least. Or at least for certain categories of apps, like games, or everything but streaming TV apps, if that was their original area of concern.

Apple TV could be a more interesting living room platform if it wasn’t hobbled by these kinds of restrictions. Prohibition against web browsers is another foolishness.

9to5Mac independently confirmed that an Apple TV app is force-quit by the system when it allocates more than two gigabytes of memory for its process. The developer API os_proc_available_memory function also reports a 2 GB limit to the app, the same value as the third-gen Apple TV.

It is unclear whether this is an intentional policy decision, or an oversight. Nevertheless, the 2 GB limit is the status quo. Tangentially, it’s worth noting that the 128 GB of onboard storage is also not usable by a single app or game; tvOS imposes app bundle limits of about 4 gigabytes with apps able to reserve about 20 GB extra for some assets.

Regarding the unchanged RAM limit despite doubling the internal memory on the chip, there is some speculation that Apple opted to reserve a portion of the system memory to help the performance of the Siri AI models. However, this doesn’t make too much sense to us. The most complex Siri AI features you can do on the TV offload to a connected iPhone or server backend anyway. The same Siri AI features are also available on the prior two generations of Apple TV hardware, so it doesn’t seem like RAM constraints are a meaningful factor.

One group of users hoping for more RAM in the Apple TV was the game decomp community, which use AI to get AAA studio games running on anything from an Apple TV to an iPhone. Some of their projects have run into the 2GB tvOS limit previously, and were hoping that the new Apple TV would alleviate that. So far, that is simply not the case.

Motorsport recorded 1.5 million sales of downloadable content (DLC), which offers extra digital features for its primary racing title. This strategy generates ongoing revenue from existing players who don't need to buy an entirely new game.

Positive cash generation allowed Motorsport to pay down vendor debts and repurchase equity while accumulating $5.4 million in cash. With a healthier balance sheet, management can fund new product development rather than manage for short-term liquidity.

Proprietary network infrastructure and an in-house web portal give the business direct ownership of its customer relationships. Executive attention's shifting toward portfolio diversification and long-term capital discipline.

With legacy liabilities resolved and recurring subscription streams expanding, the strategy pivots from restructuring to product growth.

#3104. Apple engineers ‘actively working’ on Face ID for iPhone Duo 2’s outer display: report

Next fall, Apple will introduce its second-generation iPhone Duo. It’s unclear what it’ll offer in terms of meaningful upgrades outside of the usual chip upgrades and camera improvements, but Apple engineers are reportedly attempting to bake Face ID into the device. That said, the feature might not make the cutoff.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has two priorities for iPhone Duo: Face ID and the Action Button. The latter might just end up being a new software addition to Camera Control that allows you to remap the hold action from Siri in Camera to an app of your choice.

As for Face ID, Apple engineers are ‘actively working’ on integrating the technology on the device, specifically on the outer display:

Other goals for the next couple of generations include adding a telephoto camera and making the device thinner and lighter overall. But Face ID is the top priority. I’m told that Apple has already developed prototypes of the iPhone Duo 2 with Face ID, and engineers are still actively working to integrate the facial-recognition system into the outer display of the second-generation model.

That said, the feature might not make it. According to Gurman, the timelines are tight here and it isn’t quite ready – so he isn’t reporting with certainty on whether or not this feature will make it. If it doesn’t debut with the iPhone Duo 2, it’ll likely be in the cards for iPhone Duo 3 in 2028.

Later down the road, the company wants to introduce an improved camera system for the iPhone Duo, including a telephoto camera. It also wants to make the device even thinner and lighter. The Duo definitely needs to be lighter, but making it even thinner would be an interesting feat.

While Face ID on the iPhone Duo would certainly be much appreciated, I’m not quite convinced that it’ll be super meaningful on only the outer display.

So the front display will have Face ID but the inner display won’t. That’s gonna be frustrating for some.

I’m fine with Touch ID, but whenever it is bothersome, it’s usually on the inner display, where it can be hard to reach the button depending on how you’re holding the device. If I could only have Face ID on one display, I think I’d rather have it on the inner display.

Orientation can make a huge difference for how you reach Touch ID on the inner display, whereas you’re generally only going to hold the outer display one of two ways: upright in your left hand, or upright in your right hand.

#3103. Here’s one small change that could improve iPhone Duo’s unoptimized apps

iPhone Duo has been out for about 3 weeks now, and I’ve happily been using mine since launch day. Many people have made a big deal about the app situation, but I’d largely say most apps I rely on are updated for iOS 27.0 at least.

That said, a fair number of apps are still from iOS 26 and earlier, and those apps have letterboxing. In my time since trying the phone, I feel one quick adjustment could make the letterboxing a lot less of an issue.

Right now, on the home screen, iPhone Duo allows you to long press an app and open it in Split View. All iPhone Duo apps allow Split View, even if the developer hasn’t compiled it for iOS 27 or 27.1.

One of the beautiful things about iPhone Duo Split View is the fact that you don’t have to decide what you’re splitting right away. On the other half of the display, you’ll see your home screen, and you can later decide what app to open.

So, given the fact that a non iOS 27 app will only occupy around half of the inner display anyways, I feel like it’d make sense to have an option to open every non-optimized app in Split View by default – rather than needing to select it every time. Or, better yet, toggle certain apps to always open in Split View.

Certain apps, even if they’re optimized for iOS 27, don’t quite feel right spread across the wider inner display of iPhone Duo – so it’d be nice to always have them in a half split without needing to think about it.

This would be a small UX improvement that I feel would go a long way, so if Apple could implement this on iPhone Duo – it’d certainly help out the app situation. While they’re at it, it’d be nice to have Slide Over on the iPhone Duo, for when you want to quickly see a smaller app on top of your full screen app.

#3102. SoFi Expects About 50% Earnings Growth in 2027 and Says It Won't Need to Raise New Capital

The online bank's growth is now being earned rather than bought. This is a key turning point for investors.

There's no denying that SoFi Technologies' (SOFI -1.34%) growth story is a compelling one. But there's also no denying that it has issued a bunch of stock to fund this growth. Since its mid-2021 public offering, this online bank's outstanding share count has grown from 365 million to nearly 1.4 billion, with another $1.5 billion worth of SOFI shares created and sold just at the end of last year...55 million shares at $27.50 apiece. Given its history, some investors are understandably worried another round of dilutive fundraising is in the offing.

However, SoFi's capital-raising days may finally be in the rearview mirror, with growth being self-sustaining using just its current cash flow.

That's the word from CFO Chris Lapointe anyway, who said as much during October's Q3 earnings conference call when laying out SoFi's earnings growth projections for the year ahead.

SoFi Technologies didn't leave investors wondering anything. Based on its results through the third quarter, the company upped its 2026 full-year revenue guidance to $5.04 billion, up 40% from 2025's top line. It's also now calling for per-share earnings of $0.61 versus last year's $0.39, up from Q2's expectation of $0.60 per share.

With a relatively tough 2026 -- which saw the loss of some of its institutional platform business -- on the verge of coming to a close, the company finally expects its true growth rate to start shining through. A revenue projection of $6.4 billion for 2027 is a 27% increase over this year's projected sales, and with this ever-growing scale SoFi anticipates net income of $1.28 billion next year, or a profit of $0.90 per share, up 47% from this year's expected per-share bottom line.

It can do it. The company's already on the right trajectory, driving 35% year-over-year growth in customer headcount in Q3 -- adding a record-breaking 1.2 million customers during the three months ending in September -- yet growing its total active products/services usage 44% higher as more than half of product sales were made to existing customers. The organization simply needs to continue doing what it's doing, which is making more and more consumers comfortable with the idea of a bank without brick-and-mortar branches.

The million-dollar question, of course, is whether this self-sustaining profit growth is already fully reflected in this ticker's price, or if there's upside potential from here? Priced at just over 17 times next year's expected per-share profits, some of this growth is indeed already factored in. Most of it isn't, however, particularly given what's likely after 2027.

With only 17.1 million customers onboard, versus roughly 270 million adults living in the United States, there's room for growth. Indeed, longer term, the company's 2030 goals imply at least $8 billion in revenue, although it could conceivably be doing considerably more business by then. #3099. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on these 3 stocks for strong long-term growth potential

Global stock markets have been volatile as investors continue to assess geopolitical risks in the Middle East, fundamentals and valuations of companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) market and key economic data.

Top Wall Street analysts help investors look past near-term noise and pick attractive stocks with solid long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Credo Technology (CRDO) provides high-speed connectivity solutions for AI data centers. Robust AI-led demand for the company's copper and optical interconnects has boosted revenue, driving a solid year-to-date rally.

In his latest research report, Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya raised his price targets on major semiconductor and semiconductor capital equipment stocks, with the price target for CRDO jumping to $340 from $252 with a reiterated a buy rating.

The 5-star analyst noted that Credo is seeing continued strength in the demand for its AECs (active electrical cables) from major and emerging hyperscalers. Moreover, the company has additional growth opportunities in optical DSPs (digital signal processors), ZF optics, ALCs (active LED cables), and PCIe retimers. These products are expected to begin ramping up production and profits in 2027-2028.

Following a meeting with the company at the 2026 BofA Global Tech Conference, along with recent channel checks, Arya raised his sales outlook for Credo by 2%-11% for fiscal 2027-2028 and his earnings per share (EPS) outlook by 5%-15%. The improved estimates reflect a strong AEC market outlook over the next five years and the company's "bulletproof reliability and incremental nature of its optical portfolio."

Arya based his new price target on a price-to-earnings multiple of 34x 2028 earnings, compared to the prior valuation of 33x 2027 earnings, saying it reflects contributions from new product adoption in coming years.

Arya ranks No. 84 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 62% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.5%. See Credo Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

Next on this week's list is Facebook- and Instagram parent Meta Platforms (META). Recently, Meta introduced consumer and business paid subscription plans for its Family of Apps and a new suite of Meta One (AI) subscription offerings.

Following the launch, Evercore ISI analyst Mark Mahaney reiterated a buy rating on META with a price target of $930. Mahaney views the rollout of the new subscription plans as a revenue diversification initiative, which could have a modest impact on revenue and eventually an even greater impact on operating income.

The 5-star analyst explained that he doesn't expect these new offerings to significantly affect near-term revenue growth due to their phased rollout and potentially low initial conversion rates. But he believes that even modest adoption within Meta's massive user base (over 3.6 billion daily users) could evolve into a significant high-margin revenue stream over the long term.

Mahaney highlighted that META is among Evercore ISI's top three, large-cap long-term picks, alongside Amazon and Spotify. His channel checks remain positive on Meta. Moreover, Mahaney noted that the Mark Zuckerberg-led company is successfully using AI to enhance user and advertiser satisfaction, reflected in engagement and return on ad spend (ROAS).

"What we now have with Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp Plus subscriptions is another attractive greenfield monetization opportunity for Meta – one that is not captured in Street estimates," concluded Mahaney, adding that his 2028 revenue estimate is 5% above Wall Street's consensus projection.

Mahaney ranks No. 987 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 53% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.8%. See Meta Platforms Financials on TipRanks.

Another social media platform in this week's list is Pinterest (PINS). Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris recently reiterated a buy rating on PINS with a price target of $24, citing "continued usage health and strengthening U.S. advertising business, each supported by ongoing AI-powered improvements."

The 5-star analyst highlighted that Pinterest has delivered double-digit global user growth for ten consecutive quarters, with his May data analysis indicating particular momentum in the second quarter of 2026. Morris said his Q2 2026 revenue growth estimate is at the high end of the company's guidance range.

Notably, Morris expects double-digit top-line growth in the United States and Canada to continue as large retailers adapt to new tariffs and the company's heightened focus on mid-market/small- and medium business advertisers expands its revenue base.

Morris believes that the adoption of Pinterest's Performance+ AI-powered advertising offering remains a major growth catalyst, currently accounting for 30% of lower-funnel revenue. The analyst sees scope for further penetration of this tool as advertisers using the product are increasing spending at nearly twice the rate of non-users.

Furthermore, Morris believes that the tvScientific acquisition expands Pinterest's reach into connected TV advertising, expanding the value of the platform's users offsite. #3098. Nike’s First Investor Day in 9 Years Is Days Away: 3 Numbers You Need to Know Before Nov. 17

The market wants clarity regarding management’s long-term plan to drive financial success at the storied company.

It has long held a leadership position in the global sportswear market. But Nike (NKE +0.61%) shares have been on a losing streak, and investors are starting to lose patience. The turnaround effort under CEO Elliott Hill is taking longer than anticipated.

The company had its last investor day in 2017. Its next one is scheduled for Nov. 16 and 17. During the two-day presentation, Nike will provide investors with critical updates about the direction the business is headed. Management will discuss its growth objectives and strategic priorities.

Before being flooded with a fresh look at Nike's outlook, here are three numbers you need to know about this consumer discretionary stock.

Nike is trying to recapture its edge. Product innovation has been a weak point in recent years, with the business leaning too heavily on its classic footwear designs. This doesn't drive excitement among customers, who are always chasing new trends in the world of fashion. The success of budding rivals in an already competitive industry has made things even more difficult.

That backdrop continues to pressure the top line. For fiscal 2027, executives expect that Nike's revenue will register a high-single-digit percentage dip. If this forecast holds true, it would follow flat sales in fiscal 2026 and a 10% decline in fiscal 2025.

The situation is even worse in the Greater China segment. What was Nike's fastest-growing market in the past, a country it has operated in for 45 years, has now turned into a major financial drag. During the most recent fiscal quarter (first-quarter 2027 ended Aug. 31), revenue there fell 22% year over year to $1.2 billion. Consumers are favoring local brands over Nike.

Investors once loved having Nike in their portfolios. During the five-year period leading up to their all-time high on Nov. 5, 2021, shares had climbed an impressive 255%. This easily outpaced the broader market. Nike benefited from surging profits.

The mood on Wall Street has soured, as market sentiment has turned sharply negative. At the peak, Nike sported a market capitalization of $281 billion. Today, that figure sits at $56 billion. The stock price trades 79% off its record (as of Nov. 12).

This pessimism is reflected in the valuation. Shares sell at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 18.2. At first look, this doesn't appear to be a bargain. Over the past 10 years, however, Nike's stock has rarely been cheaper.

Even more surprising is the share price. At $38, shares are roughly at the same level where they stood all the way back in 2014. Nike was generating significantly less in revenue around that time.

Contrarian investors will view this as a favorable setup. Nike might only need to introduce small fundamental improvements in order for market sentiment to make a positive shift.

If you're an income investor, Nike presents a very compelling opportunity. Because the stock has tanked over the past five years, the quarterly payout of $0.41 has a much bigger effect. The dividend yield is strong at 4.3%. This is substantially higher than what some blue chip dividend stocks offer investors.

The dividend's sustainability is something to be mindful of though. I don't believe there is a lot to be concerned about in this regard. Despite its struggles, Nike remains profitable. Its balance sheet is in solid shape, with sizable cash.

Last November, the business raised its quarterly payout by 3%. This was the 24th straight year it did that. If history is any indication, the board of directors will implement another hike this month. Income-seeking investors can be encouraged by that superb track record. It demonstrates Nike's commitment to its shareholders.

#3097. How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain – and what you can do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

New research provides a stark look at the AI supply chain and the risks it brings to businesses.

Artificial intelligence companies worldwide are bringing a new wave of vulnerabilities and security issues to the digital supply chain, researchers warn.

According to a new report published by Black Kite on Tuesday, there now exists a “widespread cybersecurity weakness” across the “rapidly expanding ecosystem of companies developing, deploying, and supporting artificial intelligence.”

AI and smart solutions don’t automatically equate with safe solutions. In a study titled “2026 AI Supply Chain Report: The Risks Behind Your AI Relationships,” Black Kite says that many AI suppliers — the companies that develop and deploy AI services to today’s businesses — are struggling with “basic security practices.”

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

According to the research, after examining the companies themselves, along with their software, integrations, and components, researchers found failures to patch critical vulnerabilities, protect credentials, authenticate users and email, and address network security issues.

The study analyzes 18,160 AI companies worldwide, ranging from 0-10 employees to more than 1,000 employees. A company’s AI involvement was determined through reviews of company products and services and primary business activities, covering six broad groups: everyday application development; AI development and implementation; AI applications in specialized sectors such as healthcare, IT, and finance; industrial organizations; and AI foundations working on data, compute, and modeling.

A small percentage of assessed companies are considered “unclassified,” and the study excluded businesses that use AI only incidentally.

In addition, unusual network activity was detected at 44.3% of organizations, and botnet-related activity was recorded at 41.8% of AI companies.

AI’s main business appeal is its ability to integrate with existing software and platforms to handle manual tasks, heavy lifting, and tedious, time-consuming work, freeing employees to focus on work that requires human oversight.

Enterprises are investing billions of dollars in AI. Menlo’s 2026 research estimates that enterprise AI spend reached $37 billion in 2025, with half of overall spend going to AI apps. In total, 76% of enterprise AI solutions are purchased rather than built internally.

However, the moment an AI or automated component is introduced into a corporate ecosystem or operational platform, any security problems it has impact the user — and each additional integration, such as software components or open-source tooling, may also increase the attack surface.

In an accompanying analysis of AI firms’ use of Model Context Protocol (MCP) components, which can link AI apps to business systems, 48.8% of 1,732 logged security findings were rated High or Critical, including code and command injection vulnerabilities.

Also: The new enterprise AI expert every company needs

It’s not just the AI application itself. As noted by Black Kite, AI suppliers often have access to customer data, developer environments, business infrastructure, and enterprise platforms. If the supplier’s credentials are stolen, this could expose its customers to a range of cyberattacks.

The researchers found, for example, that 19.9% of AI companies offering solutions for enterprise AI deployment had corporate login information in infostealer records, and that stolen corporate logins, overall, were linked to 6.8% of AI suppliers in the study.

Visibility matters, too, for businesses that should be monitoring their digital supply chains. However, 33.2% of AI companies assessed have a “limited” digital footprint, including their domains, subdomains, and IP addresses.

The same principles for protecting the digital supply chain apply to AI suppliers, where continual monitoring and assessment are among the best protections businesses have.

Staying informed and aware of the risks to your own business makes all the difference. As recommended by Black Kite, it takes more than a single point-in-time security assessment — frequent monitoring and engaging with suppliers to understand their technologies and dependencies can reveal potential security issues.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance?

If you find weaknesses, manage them by priority, handling ransomware-related exposures and vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild first.

Also audit an AI tool’s integrations and components, access, what data it can reach, and the potential impact of exploitation. Once you’re armed with this information, it’s possible to weigh risk and reward — and whether the AI tool is worth the potential attack exposure it brings. If you decide to keep it, limit its permissions and access to what it requires.

There will be daily updates capturing all the highs and lows of camp life, including those all-important Bushtucker Trials. Episodes will air every evening from 9 p.m. GMT (4 p.m. ET / 1 p.m. PT), with the finale being broadcast on December 7.

Production takes place in Dungay Creek, located in Murwillumbah, New South Wales, where the series has been filmed for the majority of its 24-year run.

Avid viewers will want to turn over to ITV2 to watch "I'm a Celebrity: Unpacked" after daily episodes of the main show end. Hosted by Sam Thompson and Kemi Rodgers after Joel Dommett stepped away this year, the companion show is available to watch on the linear ITV2 channel, or live and on-demand with ITVX's free streaming service.

Live streamer and YouTuber Angryginge became King of the Jungle last year, with "Celebs Go Dating" presenter Tom Read Wilson the runner-up and actor/singer Shona McGarty completing the finalists.

#3095. Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things – even upstairs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Home Security

Alongside the Ring Drone Cam, Ring introduced the Rover Cam for businesses. It investigates disturbances and streams 4K footage.

Today, Ring announced the launch of a new subbrand, Ring Robotics, with two new products: the $249 Ring Drone Cam, an indoor “mobile security camera” drone that shoots 2K video, and the $999 Ring Rover Cam, a security robot for businesses that patrols autonomously and investigates disturbances.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home

Both devices use Ring’s custom navigation software, “AI Pilot,” to autonomously navigate interior spaces and move between set points along a patrol, rather than being controlled directly by the user. AI Pilot leverages the devices’ cameras, sensors, and vision models, along with cloud processing, to create interior maps, then move the devices between predesignated patrol points such as a side door or a window.

I recently saw both new robots in person at a showcase in New York hosted by Ring’s founder and chief inventor, Jamie Siminoff. They certainly do what they advertise but come with some significant limitations. The drone, for example, can only stay in the air for about 8 minutes before it needs to dock and recharge, while the Ring Rover Cam is slow and deliberate, seemingly ideal for routine surveillance rather than rapid response to an event.

The Ring Drone Cam moves around predetermined patrol points in your home, sending you a live 2K video feed whether you’re just in another room or out of town. The user doesn’t actually fly the drone; instead, it moves around autonomously using Ring’s custom “AI Pilot” navigation technology, leveraging its cameras, sensors, and cloud processing to create a map of its surroundings. This allows it to fly through the air at an appropriate height, going from room to room, even up stairs.

In the Ring app, the user creates patrol points they want the drone to move between — likely a window, doorway, or high-traffic room — creating a set path that is both predictable (so you always know where the drone will go) and relevant, so it’s only monitoring the areas you want it to. But here is where its limitations come into play: It needs a finite path to navigate because its flight time is limited to just five to eight minutes in the air before it has to return to its charging dock.

That makes the dock both the start and end point for the drone’s routine trips, and it’s designed with this in mind. When it goes to land, the drone hovers over the dock and lowers itself down, dropping into place so it can start charging automatically. I asked about its potential to land elsewhere, and Ring told me it would only make an emergency landing outside of its dock in case it didn’t have enough power to get home.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Dot can turn into a Wi-Fi extender – how it works

There’s one other very important caveat: This thing is loud. There’s no sneaking up on anyone with the Ring Drone Cam, as the entire household is likely to hear it the second it undocks. The four propellers emit a constant, high-pitched whirring while in the air that’s loud enough to announce its presence to anyone in the vicinity: intruder or resident.

During the product briefing, Siminoff insinuated that this was part of its design to dissuade home intruders snooping around your house at night (especially when paired with the drone’s front-facing spotlight), but it’s likely just the result of its engineering, especially considering this is a first-gen product. It’s so loud that it makes me think it’s better suited to navigating the home when no one’s home (although whether or not your pets go bonkers trying to catch it is a whole other issue).

The Ring Drone is designed to work out of the box with the existing Ring ecosystem, including the 2K Video Doorbell and Indoor Cam, and is also compatible with Amazon’s Map View.

The Ring Drone Cam will start shipping on Jan. 27, 2027, and will cost $249.

The other product Ring announced is the Rover Cam, a mobile robot with a 4K camera designed to monitor large spaces like warehouses, offices, or businesses. Ring calls it a “security guard that never clocks out,” but it’s more like a slow-moving droid that goes on set patrol paths. It leverages the same AI Pilot technology as the Ring Drone to map its surroundings and navigate around shelving, furniture, and obstacles in real time.

It’s much quieter than its airborne sibling, traveling at low speeds and offering mobile surveillance instead of wiring every square inch of a large space. If the technology here looks familiar, it’s because it resembles the Amazon Astra, a smaller robot designed for home monitoring but with a very similar build.

The idea here is to deploy the robot to certain areas of a workplace via the app, then get 360-degree views once it’s there. Like the drone, it can also set out on automated routes at select timing intervals — like right after a business closes or before it opens. During working hours, it chugs along with its camera, capturing everything in its view.

Also: The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from today

If another Ring device is triggered, the Rover Cam autonomously goes to investigate the disturbance, providing 4K footage in real time via the app. It also features a periscope camera that can extend to see over obstacles like shelving, counters, or furniture, providing a high-level view if needed. In case you lose it in a large warehouse or office, it has a “light tower” that projects light upward onto the ceiling, notifying users of its location.

Even when docked, it uses motion-sensing technology to start recording the second it senses any kind of movement, just like Ring doorbell cameras. In case of an emergency, the Rover features a siren and red flashing lights to dissuade intruders.

The Ring Rover Cam is available for preorder now and will start shipping on Dec. 16, 2026. It will cost $999.

#3094. Laird Superfood: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Gross margin fell 7 points to 29.6% as acquired Terrasoul product lines and organic cacao costs weighed on profitability.

On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 12, 2026, Laird Superfood (LSF -7.35%) announced net sales reached $42 million. The functional food maker is expanding its product footprint into major retail channels while working to turn acquired brands into a profitable scale platform. Three things management said stand out.

Management is choosing to step up brand spending to capture demand from consumers switching to powdered coffee and those using glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) weight-loss medications who seek nutrient-dense foods. To support this growth push, Laird Superfood is deploying top-of-funnel campaigns across online marketplaces and retail accounts.

Gross profit reached $12.4 million, but gross margin (the portion of revenue left after production costs) compressed by 7 percentage points to 29.6%. Commodity cost inflation and lower-margin product lines from Terrasoul drove the contraction, which management is countering through active cost containment.

E-commerce accounted for 54% of total net sales during the quarter, up from $20.5 million to $22.5 million as online marketplaces expanded. Laird Superfood is utilizing Terrasoul's fulfillment and advertising expertise to scale its broader brand portfolio across digital storefronts.

Net sales guidance for full-year 2026 stands between $135 million to $140 million as integration work continues across supply chain network facilities and enterprise resource planning (ERP) software systems. Platform scale gives the leadership team wider choice in strategic deal selection while maintaining pricing discipline across retail accounts.

Full-year adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, adjusted for non-recurring items) is expected to arrive between $5 million and $6 million, supported by an unlevered balance sheet holding $17.3 million in cash. Strategic capital backing allows management to execute its long-term strategy.
